items.content:
If I wanted to become a Negotiation Ninja in 2026...

I'd follow this 7-step program for the next 90 days

1. One uncomfortable conversation every day 
Most people hide behind emails, decks, and "circling back." I'd force at least one real, uncomfortable conversation daily. Face-to-face or phone only. No written excuses. The more direct, the better. If it makes my stomach flip, it's the right conversation.

2. Break down real-life deals, not theory 
Books are fine, but the real gold's in the deals we close (and lose). I'd sit down with my team and dissect recent negotiations. What worked? Where did we fold too soon? Where did the other side outplay us? What warning signs did we ignore? Patterns hide in plain sight.

3. Train silence like a skill 
I'd use the ten-second rule after every major offer or request. No talking. Let the silence do the work. Most people jump in and fumble their leverage. With practice, that dead air becomes an advantage.

4. Make one bold ask per week 
Nothing reckless. Just one meaningful ask that stretches my comfort zone. Maybe it's a bigger price, tighter deadline, or extra concession. Even if it gets shot down, the learning's in the attempt.

5. Log every negotiation 
Not just the outcome. The moves. The emotions. The triggers. What did I fear? Where did I hesitate? After ninety days, this log becomes a playbook of my own weaknesses and edge.

6. Get feedback from the "no's" 
Every "no" comes with intel. Instead of chasing the win, I'd ask lost deals for feedback. Their objections, doubts, and friction points are where your blind spots are hiding.

7. Operate like every move is public 
Assume every conversation will end up on the front page of your company's website or CEO's desk. Would I be proud of how I treated the other side? Would I want my team to copy my approach? That's the standard.

You don't become a world-class negotiator by reading more books or finding the perfect script. 
You get there by practicing deliberate discomfort, over and over, until hard conversations feel normal.

Anyone can negotiate when it's easy. 
But the ones who keep leveling up? They run toward the friction.

Don't overcomplicate it. 
One habit, one day at a time. That's how you vault past everyone still playing it safe.

I thought I had a great business relationship.

This 30-second test made me think again.

Imagine you have a genuine business emergency.

You need to speak with your business partner.

Right now.

What happens next?

1-You call their cell.

They pick up and say:

“I am in a meeting. Give me two minutes to step out.”

You have an iconic relationship.

2-You text them first.

“Can I call? It is urgent.”

They respond immediately.

You have a very strong relationship.

3-You do not have their cell number.

You send an email.

You find a time for a virtual call.

You have a good relationship.

4-Your admin contacts their admin.

They compare calendars.

They eventually find a mutually convenient slot.

Ask yourself:

Do you really have a relationship?

Or do your companies simply do business together?

The real strength of a partnership is not visible when everything is going well.

It becomes visible when something goes wrong.

In those moments, trust removes friction.

My manager kept giving me extra unnecessary work.

Years later, I discovered his hidden agenda.

Message 5/22: To the Nikhil who kept asking, "Why do I have to do this?"

Message in short: 

Do not optimize your early career for less work. 

Optimize it for more capability.

My first manager, Ravishanker Begari, had a phrase I still remember:

"Your skills are your passport to success. You can only travel as far as your skills allow you."

And he practiced what he preached.

If company policy required a contract only above a certain spend, Ravi would sometimes ask us to write one for much smaller projects.

If a sourcing strategy was not technically required, we might still create one.

At the time, I found it frustrating.

Why do extra work when the policy does not require it?

Years later, I understood his hidden agenda.

He was not trying to get more work out of me.

He was trying to build more capability into me.

Every extra contract was practice.

Every extra sourcing strategy was practice.

And that practice compounded.

I eventually became qualified at advanced levels in those skills.

Today, I teach many of them as a Master Trainer.

The work I once questioned became part of the expertise I am known for.

So, to the younger me:

Stop asking:

"Do I have to do this?"

Start asking:

"What capability could this build in me?"

Because the best time to build a skill is not when your career finally demands it.

It is years before.

#22MessagesToMyYoungerSelf

items.content:
22+years. 1 company. Some say Lazy. Some say Loyal.

Today, I reveal the 6 reasons why it’s been a great deal.

When people hear I’ve spent more than two decades at P&G, they usually make one of two assumptions.

“You must really love stability.”

Or worse...

“You got comfortable.”

I don’t blame them.

A résumé tells you where someone worked.

It rarely tells you why they stayed.

Looking back, I don’t think I’ve stayed because of the company alone.

I’ve stayed because, time and again, P&G has fulfilled six fundamental human needs that all of us are searching for in our careers.

1. Certainty
Knowing I was part of a company whose values I trusted, even when the business around me was changing.

2. Variety
Moving across India, Thailand, and the U.S. From media to packaging. From sustainability to AI. From procurement transformation to ecosystem partnerships. The company stayed the same. My career never did.

3. Significance
Being trusted with problems that mattered. Not just reducing costs, but building partnerships, driving business growth, advancing responsible sourcing, and helping shape what I believe is the Procurement of the Future.

4. Connection
Working alongside mentors, leaders, teammates, suppliers, and partners who shaped not only my career, but who I became as a person.

5. Growth
Every few years, I found myself in a role where I felt like a beginner again. New countries. New industries. New technologies. New challenges. Those moments of discomfort became my greatest teachers.

6. Contribution
Realizing that the most meaningful work isn’t what you accomplish while you’re there. It’s what continues after you’ve moved on—leaders you’ve developed, capabilities you’ve built, partnerships you’ve strengthened, and systems that continue creating value long after you’ve left.

Has every one of those 22 years been easy?

Not even close.

There were failures.

There was difficult feedback.

There were moments when leaving would have been the easier choice.

But I’ve come to believe something.

A great career isn’t built by changing companies every few years.

Nor is it built by staying for decades.

It’s built by continuously becoming a better version of yourself.

For me, P&G has simply been the place that kept giving me reasons to become that next version.

Maybe that’s what real loyalty is.

Not staying because nothing changes.

Staying because you never stop changing.

Which of these six human needs has had the biggest influence on your own career?
#pgemployee

items.content:
Almost every week, I run my work past my 10Y daughter, Ira.

Not because I want her to go into procurement.

She's not a future buyer in training.

She couldn't care less about suppliers, contracts, or any of the stuff I obsess over.

But honestly, she's my best test.

If I can explain my work in a way that makes her actually pay attention, I know I'm onto something.

If she starts zoning out or hits me with a "wait, what does that mean?", I know I've lost her.

That's when I realize I'm just hiding behind big words and business talk.

Adults will smile and nod through anything.

You toss in a few fancy terms, maybe a framework or two, and everyone acts like it all makes sense.

Kids do not play that game.
They want it simple, clear, and real.

So I'll take a complicated project and try to break it down for her.

If she's still listening by the end, I know I've actually figured it out myself.
If not? Back to the drawing board.

The point isn't to turn Ira into a mini version of me.
She'll find her own thing, and that's exactly what I want.

This is about testing myself.

Can I take all this complicated stuff and make it so clear, so obvious, that even a 10-year-old can explain it to someone else?

The real kicker: the stuff that finally lands for her is always what lands for everyone else too.

If a kid can repeat your main point, you've stripped away all the nonsense.

Try it.

Pick a kid in your life and see if you can get through to them about what you do or what you care about.

You'll get honest feedback. You'll spot the parts where you're faking it or relying on jargon.

It's tough, but you end up with something that actually sticks in people's heads.

So yeah, my secret weapon for clarity is a 10-year-old who couldn't care less about procurement.

Maybe give it a shot yourself.

You'll be surprised how much better you get at your own job.

items.content:
Our Mondays need love on Saturdays and Sundays. 

Here are 6 suggestions for a Miracle Monday Morning.

Most people treat the weekend as a time to check out. Binge, scroll, or simply drift. Then wonder why Monday hits like a truck.

But building a better Monday isn't about Sunday night panic. It's about how you set yourself up, before the week even starts.

Here's how I get ahead, without burning out:

1. Plan your upcoming week. Review your calendar. Don't just accept what's there, edit it like you mean it. Remove anything that's just noise. Add what deserves your attention. Make space for what actually moves you forward.

2. Identify one big thing you want to accomplish next week. Not just at work. Pick one for work, one for family, and one for yourself. When you wake up with a purpose, Monday isn't just another grind.

3. Give yourself a gift. Not for hitting a target or checking a box. Just for being you. Massage, movie, walk, a silent cup of coffee, something that feels like a reward from you to you.

4. Find time to truly connect. Weekdays are a blur, calls, emails, constant interruptions. Weekends give you back some control. Use it. Sit down for dinner, no screens. Break out a board game. Ask a real question and actually listen.

5. Catch up on sleep the right way. Not by sleeping in and feeling groggy, but by winding down and getting to bed early. Your Monday morning will feel completely different when you wake up rested, no bonus hours needed.

6. Journal the wins from last week. Take inventory of every role you play, parent, partner, leader, friend. Write down the small stuff. It all adds up. You'll realize you're building momentum, not just running in circles.

Nobody gets a Miracle Monday by accident. 
They're built on purpose, habit by habit, long before the alarm rings.

You can wait for motivation to show up, or you can make Monday yours, before anyone else even starts.

I spent an hour with our new Gen Z hires. 
I learned 5 lessons I can't find in any leadership book.

I walked in ready to share my experience. Stories, lessons, pitfalls to avoid. The usual playbook.

But five minutes in, I knew this was going to be different.

They asked why we do things a certain way. I gave my best reasons. They pushed for better ones.

They pointed out meetings that didn't serve a real purpose. Processes that felt dated. Tools that made sense once, but don't anymore.

That hit me. It took me years to question the status quo. They do it instinctively.

They didn't care about hierarchy or titles. If an idea made sense, it didn't matter where it came from. If it didn't, they challenged it, politely, but directly.

They craved real transparency. No polished presentations. No hiding behind jargon. They wanted the truth. Even when it was uncomfortable.

I thought I'd be the one with all the wisdom.

But I left the room grateful.

A little uncomfortable.

And honestly, more open to change than I've felt in a long time.

We are also not what we think we are. 

We are what we do. Our habits make or break us.

They watch how you show up.

Start with one small habit. Show up early. Send the note. Ask the question.

Then stack the next habit. 
You don't need grand gestures. You need repeated proof.

Responsibility isn't a mood. It's a muscle.

Over time, habits become reputation. Reputation becomes influence.

If you want different results, don't wait for your next promotion or a new project.
Change the smallest choices you make today.

In the end, you are the sum of your habits, not your hopes.

items.content:
I have made a few Career-Limiting Moves (CLMs).

This time, the 10-10-10 rule saved me.

We were locked in, voices raised, both trying to get the last word. The room was silent except for us. It felt like the meeting was about to go off the rails.

I was ready to dig in. Make my case stronger. Prove I was right.

But I forced myself to pause. I went back to a trick I picked up years ago, the 10-10-10-10 filter. Four ruthless questions:

Will this fight even matter in 10 minutes?
Will it matter in 10 days?
In 10 months?
What about 10 years?

Most conflicts crumble right away. The ego hit? Fades in under an hour. The bad meeting? Forgotten by Friday. Some things stick around for a month, but even those lose power quickly.

In reality, I can only remember a handful of moments from my career that really mattered for 10 years. Things like owning a tough decision. Backing a team member when it was unpopular. Pivoting when the data demanded it.

Arguments rarely make the list.

That day, I realized the fight was pure ego. Nothing strategic. Not worth losing trust or credibility.

So, I took a breath. I reset the conversation. I asked, What problem are we actually trying to solve here?

Everything shifted. Suddenly, it wasn't about being right. It was about moving forward.

The executive lowered his guard. We found common ground. The team left with a real solution, not just a winner and loser.

Without the 10-10-10-10 rule, I might have torched a key relationship over nothing. And that's the trap most leaders walk right into. They pick up battles that vanish in the rearview mirror, while missing the ones that change the course of their team.

The 10-10-10-10 rule isn't soft. It's ruthless. It forces you to cut through your own drama and see what actually deserves your attention.

Use it. Most fires burn out on their own. Save your energy for the rare ones that matter years from now.

What argument did you regret spending energy on? Would it pass the 10-year test?

You can't shrink your way to greatness.

Then: You hammered out contracts.
Now: You build partnerships that outlast paperwork.

Then: Cost-cutting was the headline.
Now: Impact on business outcomes is the only story anyone cares about.

Then: Procurement was a silo.
Now: If you're not enabling enterprise transformation, you're invisible.

Then: Knowing your categories gave you an edge.
Now: Orchestrating across ecosystems keeps you in the game.

Then: Tech made things easier.
Now: AI is rewriting the rules.

It's what didn't.

Trust compounds, even faster now.

Integrity? Still opens more doors than a Big Four pedigree.

Curiosity beats certainty, every single day.

The leaders who deliver the most value aren't the ones who win negotiations.

They're the ones who help others win.

You want procurement to matter?

Stop aiming to be the best at cost savings.

Start aiming to be the best at building trust, enabling growth, and connecting ecosystems.

The tools keep evolving.

The fundamentals don't.

Here's my challenge: Who will raise their hand to lead the next era?

Check your calendar for 7-9 AM and 12-1 PM. There is a secret insight hiding in plain sight 🔍

Most leaders obsess over what fills their afternoons. But the hours that quietly shape your results are hiding in plain sight.

Think about 7-9AM. 
Those are your freshest hours. Mind uncluttered. No pinging teams, no pressure to perform for anyone but yourself. 
So, what do you fill it with? 
If it's email, news, or busywork, you're starting reactive. 
If it's exercise, reading, planning, or reflection, you're choosing to get sharper before anyone else asks for your attention 💡

When I look at a leader's mornings, I can tell if they're sharpening the saw or burning through the blade. 
Most grind. Few build. 
The difference reveals itself over weeks, then months, then years.

Now look at 12-1PM. 
Everyone thinks of lunch as dead time, or worse, just another chance to clear the inbox or schedule a back-to-back call. 
But this is prime relationship time 🤝 
It's the only window when everyone else slows down. 
Are you eating alone, staring at a phone? 
Or are you breaking bread with a colleague, with your team, with someone new? 
Most breakthroughs, most trust, most "out-of-the-blue" ideas, spark in these moments. 
Not in meetings. Not in slide decks.

Here's what most won't admit: 
If your calendar is a wall of meetings from 9 to 6, but you never touch the first or midday hour, you're on autopilot. 
You're letting other people set your priorities. 
You may even be proud of how full your schedule looks. 
But the signal isn't how many calls you take, it's how intentional you are with the time nobody's watching.

Leadership is leverage. 
If you don't invest in yourself when the world is quiet, your edge dulls fast. 
If you don't invest in relationships when there's no agenda, you're just another name on an org chart.

Ask yourself: 
Are you sharpening or grinding? 
Are you connecting or just consuming?

Tomorrow, protect these two slots. 
Use 7-9AM for thinking, learning, or health 🧠 
Use 12-1PM for building real connection or just recharging, no screens, no noise.

Small move. Massive impact over time. 
The difference isn't in your title. It's in your calendar 📅

The truth is hiding there, if you're willing to look.

How do you use these two windows?

I learned this the hard way. I do not want you to.

What made me a manager didn’t make me a leader.

Message #6/22: To the Nikhil managing his first direct report...

I was a newly promoted manager.

My first direct report, Ketan, was significantly more experienced than me.

And I had a rough start.

Until then, I had built my career on things I was good at.

My intelligence.

My skills.

My ability to get things done.

Those strengths had helped me become a manager.

So naturally, I tried to use the same strengths to lead.

That was my mistake.

I was too focused on my ideas and my way of doing things.

I did not appreciate enough that Ketan had years of experience, his own perspective, and a different way of working.

Fortunately, he gave me something every new manager needs.

Patience.

And honest feedback.

I was equally fortunate to have Ravi, a senior leader who saw me stumbling and coached me through it.

Together, they taught me one of my earliest leadership lessons:

Your team does not need you to prove that you are smarter than them.

They need you to listen to them.

Respect them.

And create the conditions for them to succeed.

Years later, I became known as a strong coach and eventually a Master Trainer in people management.

The irony is not lost on me.

Something I eventually became good at started with something I initially struggled with.

So, to the younger me:

Stop trying to prove you deserve to be the manager.

You already have the title.

Now earn the trust.

Because becoming someone’s manager can happen overnight.

Becoming their leader takes much longer.

22 years. 22 messages to younger versions of me.

#22MessagesToMyYoungerSelf

That we slowly stop appreciating where we already are.

Ira wasn’t looking at my title.

She wasn’t asking what I do.

She wasn’t interested in my calendar full of meetings.

Instead, she was excited by the little things.

Meeting the people I work with.

Seeing brands she had known all her life.

Walking through an office that, to her, felt full of possibilities.

And, of course, giving the Charmin mascot a giant hug.

The same office I walk into every day...

She experienced with curiosity, excitement, and wonder.

It made me realize how easily routine dulls our appreciation.

The places that once inspired us become ordinary.

The opportunities we once dreamed about become expectations.

The people we once felt lucky to work with become familiar.

Sometimes we do not need a new job, a new title, or a new challenge.

Sometimes we simply need to see our world through a child’s eyes.

Yesterday, Ira did not just visit my workplace.

She reminded me why I am grateful to be there.

What is one thing in your life that you have started taking for granted?

What if the future has no Chief Procurement Officers?

Not because procurement shrinks.
Because it explodes.

Procurement once had one job:
Help the business buy better.

Cut costs.
Negotiate contracts.
Scan suppliers.
Tick compliance boxes.
Spot risks.

Still matters.
But let's not pretend that's the finish line.

The real action?
It's not inside your company.
It's at the edges.
Where you collide with the outside world.

Suppliers.
Startups.
Customers.
Tech partners.
Universities.
Governments.
Even whole communities.

The CPO isn't just a buyer anymore.
The job now: build ecosystems.
Huge difference.

The old question:
Can we source this cheaper?
Now:
Can we build the right ecosystem around this opportunity?

Can we get partners rowing in the same direction?
Can we spark ideas that don't show up on a spreadsheet?
Can we go beyond our walls and find value out there?
For people, planet, profit?

Can we turn "just another supplier" into a real competitive edge?

That's why "Chief Procurement Officer" is starting to sound small.
What if it's "Chief Ecosystem Officer" next?

Not because procurement is fading.
Because it's moving to the center of the business map.

From policing spend to architecting value.
From squeezing pennies to fueling innovation.
From playing defense to reshaping the whole game.

Maybe the title changes, maybe not.
But the job already has.

The procurement leader of tomorrow?
They won't just lead sourcing teams.

They design how the business creates value with the world.

It's a messy, high-stakes new game.
Most are still playing checkers when the board just became chess.

What's your take?
Does procurement fade, or does it take the whole field?

items.content:
GOOD NEWS: You think you missed the AI Bus. 
GREAT NEWS: You can leap frog using these 10 steps

1. Find the smallest pain 
Look for that annoying, repetitive task you cannot stand. Data entry. Sifting emails. Chasing down updates. Stay humble, pick one thing.

2. Grab a basic tool 
Find an off-the-shelf AI tool meant for that pain point. Minimum setup. Forget custom anything. Speed beats perfection.

3. Test it in the wild 
Put it in the hands of a small group that feels the problem. No big project teams. No endless planning. Let them use it for real work.

4. Measure something real 
Pick a metric nobody can ignore. Time saved per week. Issues avoided. Workflow speed. Keep it so simple nobody can argue with the number.

5. Show off 
Share the before and after with your boss, your peers, and anyone else who will listen. No fluff. One slide, one stat. Real work done faster.

6. Take a bigger bite 
Now you have credibility. Tackle a process that nags at multiple teams. Maybe it is customer response times, invoice approvals, or onboarding. Same process: pick the pain, pick the tool, test, measure, share.

7. Recruit an ally 
Look outside your team. Find someone in another function who hates a similar grind. Give them access to your tool or share what worked. Let them ride your coattails.

8. Teach your sharpest people 
Do not boil the ocean. Pick a handful of the most curious, action-oriented folks. Get them trained up fast, let them experiment and report back.

9. Build your win list 
For every single improvement, capture what changed: What was the pain? What did you try? What changed? Stack these stories. They become your movement's proof.

10. Pitch something bold 
Now you are armed. Use those real-world results to propose a larger AI project. You are not pitching theory, you are pitching momentum. The business case writes itself.

Everyone is busy "transforming." Most get stuck in endless meetings, pilots that never scale, slides that gather dust.

Skipping the AI bus means you are not on someone else's failed roadmap. You get to jump straight to what matters: solving problems, stacking wins, building a reputation for delivery.

Start small, move fast, go bigger only when you have proof. 
No one cares about ideas. They care about results.

So, what are you going to leap frog first?

items.content:
I always wanted my career to be a ladder. 

Thank God, it didn’t happen that way. 

It became a jungle gym, instead.

That may be one of the best things that happened to me.

For the first few years, it looked like one.

Perform well.
Move up.
Take the next role.
Climb the next rung.

Then life interrupted the ladder.

I moved into an international assignment.

It gave me cultural understanding, team leadership, and humility that no straight-line career path could have taught me.

Then I moved into a role that looked similar to something I had done before.

At that point, I needed space.

My family was going through major personal transitions, and that role gave me the stability to keep growing without breaking.

Then I tried a broadening assignment in marketing.

It lasted only a few months.

But it gave me something extremely valuable:

Clarity.

I learned what energizes me.
I learned what drains me.
I learned where I can create the most value.

Then came the move to the US.

I thought it would be a short assignment.

Six years later, I am still here.

In that time, I have bought core packaging, led responsible sourcing and sustainability, and now I am in a broadening role focused on building ecosystems and external partnerships.

None of this would have happened if I had only chased the next rung.

The ladder would have given me progression.

The jungle gym gave me perspective.

It gave me range.
It gave me resilience.
It gave me stories.
It gave me skills I did not even know I needed.

I am grateful to the leaders who saw possibilities I could not see yet.

I am grateful to my family, who stayed flexible through every turn.

And I am grateful that my career did not follow the perfect plan I once wanted.

A ladder can take you up.

But a jungle gym can make you broader, stronger, and more ready for the work that actually matters.

If you lead others, do not only design career ladders.

Design career experiences.

If you are leading your own career, remember this:

Your ideal next move may not always look like the next rung.

Sometimes the sideways move is the one that prepares you for your biggest leap.
#CareersOfTheFuture

items.content:
In 1997, Apple had 90 days of cash left.

The company that saved it was Microsoft.

Steve Jobs stood on a stage in Boston, put Bill Gates on a giant screen behind him, and told a room full of Apple loyalists that their sworn enemy had just wired $150 million.

The room booed.
The deal had some wild terms.

What Apple agreed to:
↳ Internet Explorer shipped as the default browser on Mac for 5 years
↳ A 5 year commitment to keep the Mac compatible with Microsoft Office
↳ Every open patent lawsuit against Microsoft, dropped
↳ A 5 year cross-licence on both companies' patents
↳ Joint work with Microsoft on Java and QuickTime streaming

What Microsoft agreed to:
↳ 5 more years of building Office for Mac
↳ A 3 year lock-up on its $150m of non-voting Apple stock
↳ Mac versions of its software shipped the same day as the Windows versions

Nobody was doing anybody a favour.

Apple bought a lifeline. Microsoft bought Mac desktop distribution, killed a patent war, and got to keep a competitor alive while regulators were arguing Microsoft had no competition at all.

29 years later:
Apple is worth about $4.5 trillion. 2nd most valuable company on earth.
Microsoft is worth about $2.9 trillion. 4th.

1/ Always KNOW the #1 lever

Your list has 50 things on it. 1 moves the business more than the other 49. 

I'm not saying ‘only ever work on the #1 thing!!’ - I don’t vibe with that at all. But the biggest mistake is not even IDENTIFYING the #1 thing.

For me, it was aligning incentives with sponsors to deepen relationships through longer-term quarterly/annual and ‘always-on’ campaigns (instead of shorter runs).

Going much deeper with each sponsor → results went up → renewals went up → LTV and MRR went up. 

2/ Stop being the whole company

The team went from 2 to 3, and hiring #4 this week. Solopreneur + assistant is a VERY different setup to 4 people with defined roles.

A mentor explained it was the opposite: a functioning team = more of those things.

5 AI notetakers.

The funny part: the AI notetaker winning the entire market did the exact opposite of what this cartoon mocks.

Granola is at a $1.5B valuation with 70%+ weekly retention. 
It never sends a bot to join your call.

Instead, when you join a meeting, it records at the macOS layer instead, transcribing any audio going in and out of your machine directly.

This also means it works on Zoom, Teams, Meet, etc natively because they didn’t need to build a separate bot / integration for each platform.

No awkward “Granola's Notetaker has joined the meeting.”

They do a bunch of other really clever product design magic too:

→ Plugs into your calendar so it can send a pre-call notification - one-click to join the call AND launch granola AND start transcribing.
→ Lets you (optionally) jot down a few words during your call, so it knows what matters to you, and adds a more detail on those points in its summary.
→ Gives 2-3 lines of prep for external meetings - who they are, what you discussed last time you met them, recent company news, relevant links etc

Tiny moments that make the product feel indispensable once you’ve tried it.

I've sold $500k+ in newsletter sponsorships in 24 months.

Without a sales team. 95% inbound + renewals.

Now I'm hiring my first Partnerships Manager 🤝
(Not you? Send this post to someone who should apply!)

What makes this role interesting:
→ Legendary audience: 125k (+10k/mo) readers at Google, Meta, Netflix, Stripe, etc
→ Crazy sponsor lineup: Including Atlassian, Notion, Hubspot, Clay, Vanta, Attio, PostHog, ElevenLabs
→ Constant inbound: My audience brings in leads organically - you don't cold-start from zero
→ Existing systems: Pre-built skills + agents for outbound, proposals, CRM, follow-ups etc
→ Long-game: Same commission % on new business AND renewals (you keep getting paid on what you build)

What I'm looking for:
A closer who builds. Someone who can run a $100k annual partnership call in the morning and ship an enrichment agent in the afternoon. 

Someone high-agency who can read a multi-stakeholder situation, and then drive the next 10 actions: scoping proposals, follow-ups, stakeholder mapping, partner strategy, internal coordination, expanding existing accounts, etc.

You'll own and grow our sponsorships from $40k/mo to $100k+ - new business, renewals, inbound, outbound, proposals, calls, and the CRM + automation stack underneath it.

AI-native is non-negotiable.

Ideally full-time, part-time possible.

Bonus points if you've worked in media sales (newsletters, podcasts, events etc), but open to all sales backgrounds.

Important note: Our sponsors don't see us as a media buy - they see us as a partner. They DM me for advice beyond their campaigns - their hiring, social tactics, broader strategy. This is fundamentally a relationships role, not a transactions one. The person I hire must vibe this way too.

What you get:
→ 20% commission - uncapped. No base
→ Work directly with me, fully remote from anywhere in the world
→ A pre-built sales engine to plug into
→ Front-row seat to a fast-growing internet media biz
→ Freedom to follow your curiosity and shape the role over time
→ Access to pro versions of best-in-class tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Notion, Wispr Flow etc)

If you can close AND build, full role + application in the comments 👇
